newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul banks resist government-selected presidents.
newsitem.headline: Seoul banks resist government-selected presidents.

text.p: Recent protests by South Korean bank employees over continued government interference in bank management signal growing cynicism about pledges by the government that it would not meddle in business, analysts said on Wednesday.
Acting independently, employees of three leading banks have resisted efforts to install government-selected presidents.

The heads of the three banks have resigned after their banks were linked to the Hanbo Steel Co loans-for-kickbacks scandal. Although the banks provided loans to the failed steelmaker, none of the three executives has been charged with a crime.

Under banking regulations, bank presidents must be selected by individual presidential selection committees composed of senior bank officials. The committee's selection is to be approved by the Office of Bank Supervision.
But it has been common practice for the government to appoint presidents of major Korean banks without any consultation with the committee.
Analysts said bank workers doubted the government's commitment to financial reforms. A key reform has been making bank management more transparent.

"It's illogical for the government to say it would give banks the responsibility of selecting presidents when it turns around and gives them a name that should be selected," said Henry Morris, managing director at Coryo Securities.
"If the government has the right to the selection then the process is not transparent," he said.
Officials of SEOULBANK, a local bank, have dug in their heels and refused to elect a new president.
Bank board members unanimously agreed on Tuesday not to accept the resignation of president Chang Man-hwa, whom they claim was pressured to leave because of his links to Hanbo.
"The board members decided not to accept the president's resignation to protest government meddling in bank affairs," said a SEOULBANK spokesman.
"They said his resignation was not acceptable at a time when the bank was facing hardship in business operation," he said.

Korea Exchange Bank, a leading local bank, was forced to accept a government-picked president to replace Chang Myung-sun, analysts said, while state-run Korea Development Bank (KDB) was directed to appoint Kim Young-tai, former head of the state tobacco monopoly, to replace former chief Kim Shi-hyung.
The new KDB president could not begin work until this week because employees staged sit-in protests to prevent him from entering the bank.
They said they could not accept someone with no experience in the banking business.
Analysts said some of the government-designated heads had no particular background in banking.
"This would have a huge impact on the employees' morale and depress the atmosphere at the bank," said Kim Byong-seok, a financial analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
Analysts said the advantage to the government of appointing bank presidents was obvious.
"The government-picked president would be controlled by the government," said Kim at Hannuri-Salomon.
Morris at Coryo agreed: "If you are appointed by the government, I guess you have to be loyal to the government."
Analysts said it was hard to see how the government was moving away from controlling the banking industry if it was not letting the selection committee do its job.

"If you are used to having tremendous authority and power it's nice to talk about setting up changes in the system but it must be hard to surrender the power," said a foreign analyst, who declined to be identified.
"It's hard to see how you are going to have a meaningful financial reform if you don't even let the banks' presidential selection committee function."
